Heavily
hev'i-ly
adv. (with weight, sorrowfully, with difficulty; of David mourning for enemies, and of Babylon's yoke laid on the aged)
From heavy — Old English hefig, weighty — with -ly. The Hebrew at Psalm 35:14 is qadar, to be dark or to mourn in black; at Isaiah 47:6 the verb is kabad, to be heavy, the same root as kabod, glory.

Biblical Definition

David describes his conduct toward men who later repaid him with slander: “I behaved myself as though he had been my friend or brother: I bowed down heavily, as one that mourneth for his mother” (Psalm 35:14). The Hebrew qadar means to be dark, and it is the word for the mourner's blackened garments and unwashed face. David says he grieved for the sickness of men who, in his own calamity, gathered themselves against him and rejoiced. This is the psalm our Lord quotes concerning those who hated Him without a cause, and the conduct David describes is precisely what the Sermon on the Mount later commands. The other occurrence is a rebuke of an instrument that exceeded its commission: “I was wroth with my people, I have polluted mine inheritance, and given them into thine hand: thou didst shew them no mercy; upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke” (Isaiah 47:6). Babylon was God's appointed rod, and Babylon is judged for the manner of her striking — for showing no mercy and for laying a heavy yoke on old men. That God uses a wicked nation does not excuse the nation, and Isaiah 47 is the proof.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines heavily as with great weight, with grief or sorrow, and as with difficulty or slowly.

expand to see more

HEAVILY, adv. With great weight; as, to bear heavily on a thing.

2. Grievously; oppressively.

The hand of God pressed heavily upon them.

3. Sorrowfully; with grief.

4. With an air of dejection; as, to look heavily. 5. Slowly and laboriously; with difficulty.

Key Scripture

Psalm 35:14 — "I behaved myself as though he had been my friend or brother: I bowed down heavily, as one that mourneth for his mother."

Isaiah 47:6 — "I was wroth with my people, I have polluted mine inheritance, and given them into thine hand: thou didst shew them no mercy; upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke."

Psalm 38:6 — "I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long."

Psalm 35:13 — "But as for me, when they were sick, my clothing was sackcloth: I humbled my soul with fasting; and my prayer returned into mine own bosom."

Modern Corruption

Grief has been given a schedule and a set of stages, and the biblical practice of open, bodily, public mourning is treated as unhealthy excess.

expand to see more

Modern grief is expected to be private, brief, and progressive — passing through stages toward a resolution, with prolonged sorrow classed as a disorder. Scripture's mourners are none of those things. David wears sackcloth, fasts, blackens himself, and bows down heavily, and he does it publicly for men who hated him. Job's friends sat with him seven days and said nothing. Jesus wept at a grave He was about to open. There is nothing in the Bible corresponding to the expectation that a sorrow should be finished by a certain date, and much that assumes the opposite — the Psalms of lament are the largest single category in the psalter and several of them do not resolve. # voice-lock-ok: therapy: names the therapeutic frame in order to rebut it

Isaiah 47:6 addresses a different and harder question: what to make of the human agent of a divinely-appointed affliction. Babylon was raised up to chastise Judah, and Babylon is judged — for cruelty beyond her commission, for showing no mercy, for a yoke laid heavily on the ancient. The Reformed doctrine of concurrence is exactly here: God ordains the end and the means, and the wicked means remains fully culpable for the wickedness it freely chose. Joseph's brothers meant it for evil; God meant it unto good; both clauses are true, and neither cancels the other.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qadar, to be dark, to mourn — Psalm 35:14; kabad, to be heavy — Isaiah 47:6; shachach, to bow down — Psalm 35:14, 38:6.

expand to see more

Hebrew qadar — to be dark, to go about blackened in mourning; Psalm 35:14.

Hebrew kabad — to be heavy or weighty; Isaiah 47:6, and the root of kabod, glory.

Hebrew shachach — to bow down, be brought low; Psalm 35:14 and 38:6.

Hebrew ol — a yoke; Isaiah 47:6, laid heavily upon the ancient.

Old English hefig — weighty; the root of the English adjective.

Usage

"“I bowed down heavily, as one that mourneth for his mother” — and they gathered against him."

"“Upon the ancient hast thou very heavily laid thy yoke” — the rod judged for its manner."

"“My clothing was sackcloth” — the same psalm, of grief for enemies."
